questions.question: A mobile app must create a new order record on the server by sending JSON; resending the request creates another order, so the operation is intentionally non-idempotent. Which HTTP method should the request use?
questions.explanation: GET only retrieves, and PUT/PATCH modify an existing resource idempotently. Creating a new resource where a repeated request produces another record is the definition of a non-idempotent POST.

questions.question: An API client replaces an entire user-profile document in one call; proxies may safely retry it because repeating the same request leaves identical server state. Which HTTP method performs this idempotent full replacement?
questions.explanation: PUT replaces the whole resource rather than part of it, and its semantics are idempotent: sending the same PUT twice yields the same state, unlike POST (creates anew) or PATCH (partial edit).

questions.question: A web app needs to change only a user's email field without resending the entire profile document; the request body carries just the fields to modify. Which HTTP method applies partial modifications like this?
questions.explanation: PUT would overwrite the whole resource and POST creates new ones; PATCH is defined for sending only the changed fields, letting the server merge them into the existing resource.

questions.question: A REST client issues a request naming a resource ID and carrying no body; the server replies 204 No Content because the resource no longer exists. Which HTTP method was sent?
questions.explanation: A request that removes a resource and typically returns 204 (or 200) with no content is DELETE; GET/PUT/PATCH would retrieve or modify rather than destroy the resource.

questions.question: Compliance requires encrypting an existing FTP service with TLS while keeping FTP's separate control and data channels - ruling out SFTP, which tunnels everything through SSH on port 22. Which protocol meets the requirement?
questions.explanation: Two secure variants are often confused: SFTP is a different file protocol carried inside SSH, while FTPS is classic FTP (still using separate control and data channels) wrapped in SSL/TLS, which is what the requirement describes.

questions.question: A resolver caches the answer it received for 'shop.example.com': a single 32-bit address, 203.0.113.10, which the browser then uses to open an HTTPS session. Which DNS record type supplied that answer?
questions.explanation: The answer maps a hostname directly to a 32-bit IPv4 address - exactly what an A (address) record stores; AAAA would return 128 bits, CNAME another name, and MX a mail exchanger.

questions.question: After IPv6 is enabled, 'dig' returns 2001:db8::10 for a hostname and the browser connects over IPv6. Which DNS record type held that 128-bit answer?
questions.explanation: A 128-bit IPv6 address is stored in an AAAA ('quad-A') record - four times the 32 bits of an A record's IPv4 answer.

questions.question: During the four-step DORA exchange, which message does a DHCP client broadcast first - from 0.0.0.0:68 toward 255.255.255.255:67 - before any offer arrives?
questions.explanation: DORA begins with the client, which has no address yet, broadcasting DHCPDISCOVER to locate servers; only then do servers reply with DHCPOFFER, the client sends DHCPREQUEST, and the server ends with DHCPACK.

questions.question: Two DHCP servers reply to a client with DHCPOFFER. The client then broadcasts a single message that formally accepts one offer while implicitly declining the other. Which message is it?
questions.explanation: After Discover and Offer, the third step of DORA is DHCPREQUEST: broadcasting it (rather than unicasting) both selects the chosen server and tells the declined server to reclaim its offer.

questions.question: An audit flags an NMS that polls devices with plaintext community strings. It must switch to an SNMP version supporting per-user authentication and encrypted payloads (authNoPriv/authPriv). Which version is required?
questions.explanation: SNMPv1 and v2c authenticate only via cleartext community strings; the User-based Security Model with authentication and privacy (encryption) was introduced in SNMPv3.

questions.question: SMTP delivery to example.com fails even though its website resolves fine. The sending mail server first queries DNS for the record that names the domain's mail exchangers and their priorities. Which record type is missing?
questions.explanation: An A record answers 'where is the host', but an MTA asks 'where does this domain accept mail' - that mapping, including preference values, lives in MX records.

questions.question: Outbound mail from 198.51.100.25 is rejected because the receiving server ran a reverse lookup on 25.100.51.198.in-addr.arpa and got no hostname. Which DNS record type is missing?
questions.explanation: Reverse lookups query the in-addr.arpa zone, which maps an IP back to a name via PTR (pointer) records - the opposite direction of A/AAAA records.

questions.question: In the DORA exchange, which final server message confirms the client may use the offered address and commits the lease to the server's table?
questions.explanation: Discover-Offer-Request ends with the server answering DHCPACK, which finalizes the lease; a DHCPNAK instead would tell the client the offer is no longer valid.

questions.question: A browser sends a valid session cookie, but the server responds that the request was understood and access is still refused - the credentials are valid yet the resource is off-limits. Which status code is returned?
questions.explanation: 401 means unauthenticated (log in first); 403 means authenticated or not, the server refuses access. Since credentials are already valid and access is still denied, the code is 403 Forbidden.

questions.question: Wireshark shows a browser using HTTP/3 opening UDP flows to port 443 - no TCP handshake - with encryption built into the transport itself. Which transport protocol carries the HTTP/3 traffic?
questions.explanation: HTTP/3 replaced TCP+TLS with QUIC, a UDP-based transport that bundles its own handshake, encryption, and stream multiplexing to cut latency and head-of-line blocking.

questions.question: An HTTP response is returned to a client carrying status code 206 after a Range request. What does this status code indicate?
alternatives: the server is returning only part of the resource
questions.explanation: 206 Partial Content means the server is fulfilling a Range request by returning only the requested byte range of the resource.

questions.question: A packet capture shows a host broadcasting from 0.0.0.0 port 68 to 255.255.255.255 port 67 right after booting. Which protocol is the client using?
questions.explanation: A DHCP client with no address sends DHCPDISCOVER from 0.0.0.0:68 to the broadcast address on UDP port 67 where the server listens.

questions.question: Before trusting a website's certificate, a browser queries the CA in real time to check whether the certificate has been revoked. Which protocol is it using?
questions.explanation: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) provides real-time certificate revocation status checks, an alternative to downloading CRLs.

questions.question: An administrator wants www.example.com to point to web01.example.com so the web server's name can change without updating users. Which DNS record type creates this alias?
questions.explanation: A CNAME (canonical name) record maps an alias hostname to another hostname rather than to an IP address.

questions.question: An FTP session stalls because the client's firewall blocks the server's inbound data connection. In which FTP mode does the server initiate the data connection back to the client?
questions.explanation: In active-mode FTP the client sends a PORT command and the server opens the data connection back; in passive mode the client initiates both connections.
